title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
text:
Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects.

Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units.

GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked).

Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models.

GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony

Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.
author: lasu

title: Show HN: Tern – Native macOS SSH Client in Rust/GPUI (76 MB vs. Tabby's 580 MB)
text:
On my day to day work i mostly use termius and tabby as multi project ssh tool with vault, somehow most of the features i use are just vault and password manager, and they are bulky, takes about 500mb ram for such simple program, and termius wants paid plan just to sync the vault. There are free tools but their ux is not at that level.

So i built my own simple ssh client with a little bit of my taste added, it has vault, password manager, repo sync, background gallery etc.

I have been working with rust on my hobby projects about 2-3 years and really got headaches from it, because its really hard to maintain features on rust project while fighting the borrow checker. Now with claude and some llm tools its very easy to build things, even some of the code written by agents is still slop but its fine to live with some slop. The main parts are modified from well written software.

Instead of cheap copying or writing from scratch, i copied from real world solutions with apache or mit license, well maintained and well written software that has almost no ai slop.

With some amateur level rust knowledge and some inspiration projects its really easy to build such low memory software, it only takes 85-125mb with wallpaper, mostly 80mb ram.

Here's the repo https://github.com/your-moon/tern any feedback and feature requests are welcome, i gladly answer

title: Show HN: Factory DS, A Factorio-Like Game for the Nintendo DS
text:
Hi HN, I'm Ronan. I love the Nintendo DS but ran out of games that kept me hooked, so I tried porting the kind of game I play today: a factory game in the spirit of Factorio, on a 67 MHz ARM9 with 4 MB of RAM.

I had never written code for the DS, and I built it with Claude Code. I wrote the specs, the design and the balancing, and Claude wrote most of the C. The post goes through how that worked, and through the technical parts I found the most fun:

- a 2048x2048 world that is never stored: terrain is computed from (x, y), only the player's changes are kept in a hash table - night done by changing the 256-color palette instead of redrawing the screen - power grids and pipes computed per network with union-find (there is a small step-by-step animation in the post) - trains with schedules, block signals and pathfinding, plus redstone-like logic gates - a headless Mac build of the game with a text interface, so AI agents could play ~470 test sessions and even help balance the game

You can download the ROM (English and French) and play it on a flashcart or in melonDS.

title: Show HN: Commit-Aware Router, route LLM traffic around your AI/cloud commitments
text:
LLM routers can optimize for different factors like price, latency, quality, etc. Enterprises tend to have prepaid AI credits, minimum-spend agreements, cloud commitments, or commercial ceilings across OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, Azure, and other providers. We’ll call these “AI commits”.

This project is designed to consider the state of an enterprises’ current AI commits and use it to inform LLM routing decisions alongside other common variables (price, performance, etc.). This is an early PoC built using LiteLLM.

Target audience would CFOs, Strategic Finance, FinOps, Cloud Finance, and AI Platform folks who care about making sure AI commit minimums are met, and maximums are not exceeded.

Would love any feedback from folks!

title: Show HN: Hatoba, an open-source SSH client with an AI assistant and E2EE sync
text:
I've used SSH tools for years and didn't really plan on building yet another SSH client, but I ended up building one the way I wanted. Hatoba is a desktop SSH client for Windows, Linux and macOS. It's written in Rust with Tauri 2 and MIT licensed.

Each terminal has an AI assistant panel next to it. You describe the problem, and it reads the terminal screen, runs commands, types into the shell, and reads, edits and searches files on the host to find the cause and fix it. You can approve every command and edit it before it runs, let a model you pick approve the safe ones, or turn approval off. Files it changes show a diff you can undo. It works with any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic API, local models included, and supports skills and MCP servers.

Sync doesn't go through a server of mine. Hatoba deploys a Worker and a D1 database to your own Cloudflare account and syncs hosts, keys and AI conversations through them. The free plan usually covers personal use. Everything is encrypted on the device before it leaves. Keys are derived from your master password with Argon2id, every item is encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and the Worker only stores ciphertext plus the hashes it needs to sign you in. Someone who gets hold of the whole Cloudflare account still only gets ciphertext. Sync is optional, and everything works offline without it.

The usual SSH client features are there too: groups, tags and fuzzy search, ~/.ssh/config import, ProxyJump and SOCKS5/HTTP proxies, an SFTP panel, local port forwarding, and a key vault that imports OpenSSH, PEM and PuTTY keys. There's also a dashboard showing CPU, memory, disk and network for every saved host, read over plain SSH with nothing installed on the servers. SSH is russh, the terminal is xterm.js with the WebGL renderer, and the UI is React.

I develop on Windows, so it's Windows first, with a custom title bar that supports Snap Layouts and Mica, and working CJK input methods. The Linux packages and the macOS build get far less testing on real machines. The macOS build is Apple Silicon only and isn't notarized, so macOS blocks it on first launch until you allow it in Privacy & Security. Bug reports from Linux and Mac users would help the most.

Website: https://hatoba.fog.moe Downloads: https://hatoba.fog.moe/download/

title: Show HN: Pippin – macOS High-Performance Screen Sharing Client for Linux
text:
Hi HN, I built pippin, a native Rust client for macOS's "High-Performance" Screen Sharing mode on Linux. There are lots of options that can get you usable, high resolution remote access to macOS from non-Apple devices, but until recently there were no options that did not require installing and maintaining a server on your Mac.

Apple normally restricts High-Performance Screen Sharing (HEVC 4:4:4 video, system audio, and dynamic display resizing) to Mac-to-Mac connections. A week or two ago I discovered iShareScreen (https://github.com/renegadelink/iShareScreen), which did the heavy lifting of reverse-engineering Apple's protocol into a working Python client.

I did have some performance issues using the python implementation on a few of my machines, so I used iShareScreen as a reference and built a Rust client with Claude.

title: Re: The Big Discount on Intelligence...
text:
> I think that is also the case for the teams at the Labs. Anthropic plans to tell IPO investors that they see more than $30 trillion in addressable market potential

The white collar work at mega corps is 99% garbage. It only exists because the execs build empires. Its people creating make work for themselves so they can hire more people. Why do they need empires? Because compensation is based on how many people report to you. And compensation is how you prove you are higher on the social hierarchy. Being at the top of the social hierarchy is important to primates.

The real work doesn't exist for AI to claim $30T. Without the human element of empire building, the work shrinks to a few hundred billion dollars. AI won't (hopefully) do empire building. But then the middle class disappears. Then, we'll be in hunger games.

This comment (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18022154) captures accurately how big corps work:

Let me tell a story:

Lets say you were just hired as the President of a furniture company. The owner says he knows it's good furniture but even despite huge investments they can't seem to sell any furniture. Your job is to turn things around.

You start on the factory floor. The furniture is made by a combination of machines and human workers. Some people are employed to set up and configure the machines to make furniture parts. Around 150 people work on actually making furniture, either assembling it, doing quality tests, or setting up and operating the automated machinery. Things aren't perfect, but you aren't going to make any changes on your first day so you make some notes and move on. The furniture hasn't changed much over the years, it is still basically the same as it was when the furniture store opened. The furniture gets 'improved' from time to time, you see a step stool with an alarm clock, a small safe, and a webcam built into it, but when you ask the foreman he tells you nobody has ever turned on the alarm clock or used the safe or connected the webcam on any of the step stools. People seem to mainly use the stools so they can reach things that are up high. There is a problem where sometimes people slip when the stools are wet, so they worked out how to add a nonslip pad, but the product managers have decided that the next feature will be to add scents to the stools, so you can buy a stool that smells like cinnamon or one that smells like apples. They have a big advertising campaign already paid for and they already sent out the press release announcing "ScentedStools", so the machines need to be set up to start stamping out stools that smell like "Fresh Linen" by the end of the week. There are daily status meetings to update them on the progress. If the "Fresh Linen" stools aren't being produced by Thursday they are going to start having two status meetings per day.

You hear it's someone named Jim's last day, so you set up an exit interview. Jim tells you that the bosses and people upstairs don't really know what is going on in the factory. Most days he just sits and reads the news, his "nontechnical" manager doesn't know anything about furniture or how Jim does his job so there's no way for the manager to know what is going on other than to ask Jim. Supervision primarily consists of making sure Jim is sitting at his desk and looking at his monitor. Since US labor laws don't allow Jim's manager to set specific hours for him to be at work, his manager has started scheduling 9AM meetings every day to force people to turn up. Every week or so Jim has to update some Product Managers upstairs about what is going on, and he just says they are making steady progress and comes up with some specific problem to explain why they aren't done, pretty much anything with jargon will work since nobody upstairs "could tell white oak from red oak". It takes about 5 minutes to give his status update but he's expected to stay for the entire 1 hour meeting, so he brings his laptop so he can read furniturenews.com. He says he is quitting to take a much lower paying job because he is bored and doesn't respect his manager.

Next you go upstairs to the office space and find 300 people having meetings with each other about annual plans and prioritization, writing mission statements and meeting to discuss mission statements. The 300 people upstairs are constantly in motion and complaining about how over worked they are. They each have 5, 6 or even 7 (sometimes more!) 1-hour meetings every day, but you only see them meet with each other, nobody has any meetings with anyone from outside the company, nobody has meetings with possible customers, and only very rarely do you see anyone from the factory floor in these meetings, and then it is almost always just to give a status update. None of these folks really understand furniture very well, they can't really tell good furniture from bad furniture, they literally don't know the difference between solid oak and cardboard, they don't know how long it takes or how much money it costs to build a chair. After a few days of meetings you haven't met anyone who cares about furniture at all, they all seem to want to work at the furniture factory because it pays well, or they like the prestige of being 'in furniture'. Mostly they talk about how overworked they are and make the case for hiring a few more people. If they could hire another person for their team they wouldn't be so far behind. You aren't sure what they are getting behind in, are they talking about meetings they can't attend because it conflicts with another meeting that is more important somehow? Do they need more time to work on power point slides for the next days meetings? Some of the office folks have degrees in furniture science, but none of them have ever successfully built or designed any furniture outside of little school projects.

Then you go out behind the factory and see a massive mountain of furniture stacked up to the sky. The factory workers have been building furniture every day for years. People all agree that it is good furniture, maybe the best there is. Nobody ever buys any of it. It's not sold in any stores. No hotels buy it. No businesses buy it. Lots of people are lined up as far as you can see to pick furniture out of the pile for free.

How do you fix this company?

title: Re: Show HN: RemainderBot – spends leftover Claude/Cod...
text:
Hey folks; I’m the author of RemainderBot. Given your goals and task lists, it writes PRs that complete those tasks for you using excess Claude & Codex subscription tokens.

As the founder of Bakeoff, I spend my time on customer development and engineering architecture & review. RemainderBot solves two problems for me and I suspect for many others out there:

* There are many small tasks that require a few minutes of my time and need my context, but I just don’t have the mental energy to prioritize them, do a context shift, perform a small amount of work, and finalize the results a dozen times a day.

* Some weeks I don’t get close to my Claude and Codex subscription limits. That’s a waste of what are very valuable Astra and Opus 5.5 tokens :)!

RemainderBot has consistently used my goals and task lists to identify non-obvious tasks that would move me forward. It has accomplished quite a bit - 111 PRs including customer call prep, a census of 31 GitHub orgs’ agent setup files, and standalone prototypes to demo to engineers I meet with.

You interact with it in whatever interface you use with GitHub PRs. It uses your comments and decisions on whether to merge PRs to guide which kinds of tasks and approaches it takes in the future.

RemainderBot runs either as a manual process on your machine or as a cronjob on a server. In tick (cronjob) mode, it checks how much subscription quota is left and how much time there is until the weekly reset before picking a task and creating a PR.

Here’s how you get started:

* Check that git, claude (or codex), and gh CLIs exist and are authenticated on your machine

* Clone the openremainderbot repo:

  git clone https://github.com/arimwilson/openremainderbot.git remainderbot
  cd remainderbot
  cp -n GOALS.example.md GOALS.md

  cp -n sources.example.toml sources.toml
Edit those two files with your personal goals and with sources for your task lists, respectively. Finally:

  python3 -m remainderbot snapshot
  python3 -m remainderbot run --provider claude --deadline-minutes 20 --size small
These commands will pick a task, work on it in a new branch, and will cost you a few percent of your weekly quota. Please drop a comment on what it did for you and if it got anything wrong here or in https://github.com/arimwilson/openremainderbot/discussions/6 :).

More details in the blog post - https://www.ariwilson.com/writing/openremainderbot

Hope you enjoy it!

title: Launch HN: Consus (YC F24) – LLM gateway for companies handling sensitive data
text:
Hey Hacker News! I'm Eric, the founder of Consus. We route all AI requests to ITAR restricted and controlled unclassified information (CUI) compliant infrastructure. Consus itself satisfies ITAR restrictions, and we recently completed our FedRAMP equivalency audit against the 410 FedRAMP High controls. FedRAMP High is the U.S. government’s strictest security baseline for cloud services handling sensitive unclassified data. A breach of this data could cause severe or catastrophic harm. Achieving FedRAMP equivalency, or authorization, is required before processing CUI information.

Demo: https://youtu.be/6MYxJe6P4oY

Aerospace and defense is experiencing rapid growth. Unfortunately, most companies are struggling to use AI because of necessary data protections & compliance risk. These companies can move even faster if they could use the AI tools that most other industries take for granted.

I spent most of my career prior to Consus in aerospace & defense. I launched national security payloads at SpaceX, and was an early employee at Castelion. I’ve watched first hand how compliance red-tape makes it difficult for companies to adopt new technologies and trust vendors that touch their sensitive data. For example, I worked with a satellite manufacturer that doesn’t allow any AI tools, even for non-sensitive work.

Even as AI has become extremely useful over the past 9-12 months, I was surprised by how many aerospace & defense companies refused to touch it. They could see how it could be helpful, but they were scared about model providers training on their data, violating an ITAR rule, or risk losing new business because of a failed cyber assessment. These are all rational fears.

There were a lot of ways to solve some/all of these problems, but we focused on building a compliant AI inference layer that can "plug" into any AI tool or workflow. Just as OpenRouter integrates with most tools, Consus can connect to tools like ChatGPT or Claude, open source tools including the Pi coding agent or Open WebUI, or integrate with applications built and maintained by individual organizations.

Almost no aerospace & defense company lives in all three major GovClouds (AWS, Azure, Google). When I mapped where frontier models can legally run for ITAR and CUI work, each provider had some subset of models, and each model achieved varying levels of compliance. Our customers don’t think in terms of cloud providers. They think about the data controls they require, and the model they want to use. That is why we built the compliance suffix. Under the hood, every request hits a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where keys are verified and policy is enforced before anything touches inference. Every model name must carry a compliance suffix, such as gpt-5.6-sol:fedramp-high or claude-opus-5-5:itar, and any bare model name is rejected. We never proxy to the standard commercial endpoints.

Our customers are also able to build an allowlist of models, and assign spend & model restrictions to individual users in the organization. This is all handled through our Consus Portal where teams can manage spend, keys, and policies.

A typical question we hear is why not just use Bedrock in AWS GovCloud or Azure Government directly. For small teams, just getting access to these platforms is difficult. For larger organizations, GovCloud lets you inherit some but not all of the controls needed to handle sensitive data. Also, models are split across providers: GPT-5.6 Sol is only available in Azure Government, while Claude Opus 5.5 is served through Bedrock in AWS GovCloud. If you want both, you are standing up and securing two separate government cloud environments. We run all of them behind one endpoint so customers don’t have to pick a cloud, and we handle the compliance work for each one.

Given the data sensitivities, Consus does not store any customer data at rest. All prompts and completions stay in memory only for the length of the request and are never logged or written to disk. Zero data retention is strictly enforced both on ourselves and the infrastructure/model providers. We do keep metadata on each request and response for billing and audit purposes.

Consus is not self-serve by design. ITAR requires us to know exactly who is on the other end of every key, so we verify every organization and put a contract in place before issuing API keys. We charge our customers a compliance fee starting at $40/mo/seat plus AI tokens at cost.

We are actively serving customers, and would love any feedback from security experts, or developers/engineers working in highly regulated industries!

References: API Documentation: https://gateway.consus.io/overview Security & Architecture: https://gateway.consus.io/security Compliance Details: https://consus.io/compliance
